title: Do Local Economic Conditions Lead to Mass Shootings? Evidence from Three Exogenous Shocks
affiliations: IZA Institute of Labor Economics, University of Ottawa - Department of Economics, The Australian National University and UNSW Business School

detail.title: Do Local Economic Conditions Lead to Mass Shootings? Evidence from Three Exogenous Shocks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: HREC12550 UNSW
declarations.funderStatement: None

affiliations.org_name: University of Ottawa - Department of Economics
University of New South Wales (UNSW) - UNSW Business School

detail.abstract: Do local economic conditions cause mass shootings? We first document the descriptive case for an economic explanation. Among perpetrators, 39% experienced financial distress, and 46% were not working. In county panel regressions, a one p.p. increase in lagged unemployment is associated with a 0.088 p.p. increase in the mass shootings incidence, despite a rich set of controls and fixed effects. We then test whether this association is causal using three distinct sources of plausibly exogenous local economic variation: Chinese import competition, fracking-induced economic expansions, and defense-spending shocks. Across all three designs, however, we find little evidence that mass shooting incidence is determined by exogenous economic conditions. The divergence between the descriptive and quasi-natural estimates cautions against interpreting economic factors as causes of mass shootings.

title: The Cost of Distributional Uncertainty in Fragmented Markets
affiliations: Peking University HSBC Business School and CMU Tepper School of Business

detail.title: The Cost of Distributional Uncertainty in Fragmented Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Despite dramatic improvements in U.S. equity market quality, high-frequency uncertainty regarding where liquidity resides has sharply resurged. We introduce Liquidity Distribution Uncertainty (LDU) to quantify this spatial friction across fragmented exchanges. Employing an instrumental variable approach and a difference-indifferences analysis of the SEC's Tick Size Pilot, we establish that LDU causally depletes market depth, slows executions, widens transaction costs, and worsens price efficiency. Our findings have policy relevance for the SEC's June 2026 proposal to rescind Rule 611. Finally, an LDU long-short portfolio yields an 8.08% annualized return spread, driven by elevated costs and reduced efficiency.

title: Screening Investable Equities Under a Regime-Conditional Overlay A Cross-Sectional Application of the SHIELD Risk-Off Filter to a 22-Stock Indonesian Universe, Benchmarked Against Institutional Performance Standards
affiliations: Independent Inventor

detail.title: Screening Investable Equities Under a Regime-Conditional Overlay A Cross-Sectional Application of the SHIELD Risk-Off Filter to a 22-Stock Indonesian Universe, Benchmarked Against Institutional Performance Standards

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I don't have any personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced the study.
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
Sulistyardi (2026c) develops SHIELD, a walk-forward calibrated, three-factor regime-detection oscillator that reduces the maximum drawdown of a buy-and-hold position in the Jakarta Composite Index (IHSG) from -41.5% to -8.1% while producing an out-of-sample Calmar ratio of 3.53, and proposes as an agenda item for further work the question of whether the filter's benefit is concentrated in particular constituents rather than distributed evenly across the market. This paper addresses that question directly. The regime-threshold schedule calibrated on IHSG in Sulistyardi (2026c) - without any stock-specific re-estimation, preserving the parent paper's parameter-parsimony argument - is applied as a binary risk-off overlay to the daily price series of 22 Indonesia Stock Exchange constituents (the fifteen Infobank15 banks, four coal-sector names, and three additional foreign-ownership-heavy liquid names) over the walk-forward out-of-sample window of October 2022 to September 2026. Risk-adjusted performance (Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Calmar ratio) is computed for the overlaid strategy on each constituent and compared against a formal four-tier screening threshold and against six public reference points used by institutional allocators: the S&P 500, MSCI World, a 60/40 portfolio, Berkshire Hathaway (Frazzini, Kabiller, & Pedersen, 2018), the top decile of CTA/managed-futures programs, and - as a non-audited, illustrative upper bound only - the publicly reported performance of Renaissance Technologies' Medallion Fund. One constituent, Bank CIMB Niaga (BNGA), classifies as “very investable” under the proposed criteria, with a Calmar ratio of 1.92 and Sharpe ratio of 0.81 that exceed every audited institutional reference point in the comparison set; two further constituents, Bank OCBC NISP (NISP) and Bank Mandiri (BMRI), classify as “investable.” At the trade level, the three investable-or-better constituents win 91.7% of closed buy-to-sell legs, against 66.7% for the fifteen Infobank15 banks and 31.3% for the four coal-sector names, while pooled across all 22 constituents 72.7% of sell signals precede a lower price at the next re-entry; because every constituent shares the same four regime windows, these percentages rest on only four legs per stock and are treated as descriptive rather than as independent hit-rate estimates. The cross-sectional pattern - concentration of overlay benefit in mid-to-large domestic banks and near-absence of benefit in coal-sector and consumer names - is consistent with, and offers an independent cross-sectional check on, the capitalization-structure argument for SHIELD's fixed 0.6/0.2/0.2 factor weighting advanced in Sulistyardi (2026c). The paper concludes, consistent with that paper's own stated limitations, that a single four-year out-of-sample window containing one dominant stress episode is an insufficient basis for an investment allocation decision, and sets out a validation agenda before these results should be treated as more than an exploratory illustration.

Keywords: cross-sectional equity screening, regime-conditional overlay, Calmar ratio, Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, drawdown control, institutional benchmarking, backtest overfitting, Indonesia Stock Exchange, parameter parsimony

detail.abstract: Continuous volatility scaling is a standard approach to managing concentrated equity exposure. This paper asks whether binary regime gates, rules that move exposure to cash on discrete regime signals, improve the compounding properties of a Nasdaq-100 allocation relative to continuous scaling. The empirical application is a rule-based program that has generated a live, timestamped signal track since June 2026: a gated, volatility-targeted trend core, two short-horizon mean-reversion sleeves, a defensive gold sleeve, and an episodic buy-the-dip overlay. Over September 2005 to October 2026 the program earns 22.2% gross and 19.5% net annually at 15.1% volatility, with a net excess Sharpe of 1.14 and a net maximum drawdown of-17.0%; no member of the forty-five-configuration scaling grid reaches a net Sharpe of 1.14 or a maximum drawdown as shallow as-17.0%, and the program's Sharpe advantage over the reference scaling rule is +0.31 (95% CI [+0.05, +0.59]). After matching sleeve-level volatility, gates and scaling deliver comparable Sharpe ratios, with the gated sleeve's advantage concentrated in drawdown control. A substitution test replacing the gated-core architecture with continuous scaling points in the same direction: at identical assembly volatility, excess Sharpe falls by 0.13, of which +0.08 is the gated core proper and +0.05 the window overlay (the cap raise adds a further +0.02 outside the equalvolatility comparison), and the maximum drawdown rises from-16.0% to-20.4% (-28.6% at the reference calibration), with the matched-risk differences individually within sampling variation. The program outperforms scaling in all five objectively defined stress episodes and in an approximate predevelopment extension to 2000-2005. The rule set was frozen on September 22, 2026; prospective evidence remains limited.

detail.abstract: Many communities across the U.S. are actively working to attract emerging industries to their area, but the labor market implications of these siting decisions are often not assessed against the existing composition of the local workforce. The lack of evidence of occupation-level labor market impact from new investments is a gap that is hard for economic development offices to overcome. This paper uses skill-informed measures of labor readiness to evaluate workforce compatibility between industries and counties. We evaluate six candidate industries, data centers, electrical equipment manufacturing, electric vehicle battery manufacturing, electric arc furnace steelmaking, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and plastics and ethylene manufacturing, across ten counties in Southwest Pennsylvania. We test labor supply strain at several demand levels and hiring similarity thresholds and consider wage competitiveness and skill-informed location quotients to get a full picture of the possible impact and compatibility of each industry-county pairing. Results show substantial heterogeneity in worker demand and relative wage impacts of each industry, with data centers needing the fewest workers and having the least impact on total wage bill, despite having the largest wage premium. We also find rural counties have higher strain than larger counties for all industry types, but their relative skill density is better aligned, indicating competitive advantages that can be leveraged when recruiting industries.

title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
affiliations: University of Bristol and New York University (NYU)

detail.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems-establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.

title: Do Option Prices Reflect Index Composition? Evidence from ETF Rebalancing
affiliations: Nankai University

detail.title: Do Option Prices Reflect Index Composition? Evidence from ETF Rebalancing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Rule-based ETF rebalancing provides a simple test of whether option prices reflect predictable changes in portfolio composition. Many index rules fix the rebalancing date in advance and set the new weights from prices observed one to two weeks earlier, so the post-rebalance portfolio is largely known before it takes effect. Using 640 rebalancing events for 30 U.S. ETFs, I compare the change in ETF implied volatility with a forward-looking benchmark built from constituent option prices, which accounts for how much of each option's remaining life falls under the new portfolio. ETF options adjust, but only partly. Implied volatility reflects about 40% of the mechanical change in portfolio risk, significantly less than realized volatility does. Little of the adjustment happens before the effective date, even though options traded in the preceding weeks already span the new portfolio, and a benchmark calibrated on the eve of the rebalance would make options look almost entirely unresponsive. Options on single-stock leveraged ETFs, by contrast, reprice simple pre-announced leverage changes promptly, consistent with slow aggregation of information spread across many constituents. One implication is that option-implied correlation measured around rebalances can partly reflect stale composition rather than correlation risk.

title: When Does a Tariff Pay? Theory, Two Centuries of Episodes, and the American Experiment of 2025-26
affiliations: InnovationStrat Consulting, LLC

detail.title: When Does a Tariff Pay? Theory, Two Centuries of Episodes, and the American Experiment of 2025-26

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is founder and principal of InnovationStrat Consulting, LLC, whose services include quantitative-finance advisory. The views are the author's own and do not constitute investment advice.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses only publicly available market data; no human participants, patients or personal data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Under what conditions does an import tariff raise the welfare of the country that imposes it, and how often have those conditions held? One accounting identity answers both questions. In a linear model of a single import market the welfare change from a tariff decomposes into a terms-of-trade gain and a deadweight triangle, with no third term; adding revenue, an input-cost term, a retaliation term and a market-failure correction gives a welfare ledger about which we prove eight propositions. Six further propositions extend Samuelson's 2004 Ricardian example, in which productivity catch-up abroad lowers the home country's real income for good: a tariff cannot restore that loss in the regime that produces it, gains only against a fully specialised partner until the partner answers, and has a finite optimum at the boundary between the two regimes. We trace tariffs and the exchange rate through the 1930s, 1971, 1985, 2018-19 and 2025-26, when the dollar fell 7.75 percent while the effective tariff rose. Five histories show how Singapore, Japan, Korea, Germany and China became export powerhouses, and we ask whether the United States should copy them, what the evidence says about debtor and creditor positions, and how the colonial empires and the treaty-tariff states of 1820-1950 used the tariff, giving the evidence for and against on each question. Scored against the same six entries, no episode of the twenty-four earns an overall "raised"; nine come out "lowered", nine "mixed", six "cannot say". Section 12 grades thirteen proposals for raising comparative advantage.

title: Israel, Qatar, and the Limits of Self-Defense
affiliations: Southwestern Law School

detail.title: Israel, Qatar, and the Limits of Self-Defense

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: self

detail.abstract:
This article examines the legality of Israel’s September 9, 2025 airstrike in Doha targeting Hamas leaders and argues that the operation exceeded the limits of self-defense under international law. Drawing on the United Nations Charter, International Court of Justice jurisprudence, the Caroline standard, and the law of neutrality, it assesses the strike against the requirements of necessity and proportionality and the protection of third-state sovereignty. It argues that responsibility for past atrocities and participation in an ongoing armed conflict do not, without further justification, authorize force against individuals located in another state.

The article critically evaluates the contested “unwilling or unable” doctrine, emphasizing Qatar’s acknowledged role in hosting Hamas’s political bureau to facilitate mediation and ceasefire negotiations. It also distinguishes jus ad bellum from jus in bello, explaining why the possible targetability of individuals under international humanitarian law does not independently establish the legality of using force on Qatari territory. Comparisons with U.S., Turkish, and Russian claims of self-defense illustrate the broader dangers of expansive interpretations of Article 51. The article concludes that the Doha strike violated the Charter’s prohibition on the use of force and undermined neutrality and peaceful dispute settlement. It calls for renewed protection of states facilitating negotiations, arguing that normalizing such operations threatens both the legal limits on preventive war and the diplomatic space necessary for negotiated peace.

title: From PropTech to Intelligent Real Estate: How Generative AI and Machine Learning Are Reshaping Property Management and Investment Decisions

detail.title: From PropTech to Intelligent Real Estate: How Generative AI and Machine Learning Are Reshaping Property Management and Investment Decisions

affiliations.org_name: African Center for Technology Enhance Learning,National Open University of Nigeria

detail.abstract: The real estate sector has moved from digitising transactions to automating cognition. Early PropTech applications, such as listing portals, digital leasing and smart-building sensors, improved access to information but left interpretation and judgement largely to human professionals. Advances in machine learning (ML) and, more recently, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) are shifting that boundary. This article examines how these technologies are reshaping property management and investment decision-making. Drawing on a structured narrative review of academic and industry sources, it develops a four-layer conceptual framework (data, model, decision and governance) and applies it to valuation, predictive maintenance, tenant engagement, lease abstraction, portfolio analysis and due diligence. The analysis suggests that value is concentrated where unstructured data, such as documents, images and conversations, can be converted into structured, decision-relevant signals, and that the main constraints are not algorithmic but concern data quality, model risk, bias and organisational readiness. The article proposes a four-stage maturity model and a research agenda, and argues that intelligent real estate will be defined less by individual tools than by the discipline with which firms combine machine inference with human oversight.

detail.abstract: This paper assesses whether a formally authorized, Mexican-consented U.S. campaign against Mexico’s fentanyl-producing cartels can deter those organizations, reduce U.S.-bound fentanyl supply, and damage their business. “Declared war” in the title means a public, statutory commitment to use force, an Authorization for Use of Military Force paired with a joint U.S.–Mexican ultimatum, not a declaration of war under Article I, Section 8. The paper specifies the campaign as four concurrent tracks: diplomacy and sanctions; restriction of precursors and equipment; intelligence and covert action; and strikes on the non-commercial industrial base and on the leadership of organizations that continue fentanyl production after the ultimatum, with an exit open to successors. Using a structured, focused comparison of Operation Tidal Wave II, Operation Iron Tempest, the 2025–2026 maritime strike campaign, and the 2025–2026 campaign against Iran, together with DEA laboratory data, CDC mortality data, U.S. court records, and Mexican constitutional texts, it finds that credible U.S. pressure from 2023 to 2026 changed cartel fentanyl behavior and moved Mexico toward cooperation; that strikes on transport alone displaced traffic without reducing supply; and that in Iran, strikes on fixed capital whose inputs were denied left enrichment plants assessed inoperable a year later, while decapitation produced a successor and a memorandum of understanding that broke down within ten days. The author projects a 25–45% reduction in U.S.-bound fentanyl supply in the first year. Against an intensified intelligence partnership without strikes, the marginal effect at peak is about 5,500–7,500 overdose deaths averted a year if a negotiated abandonment holds, and close to none if it does not. Mexican consent is the decisive constraint. The strategy reduces and disrupts the market; it does not eliminate it. An annex profiles the designated organizations from public records.

title: Governing Agentic AI in Finance: A Use-Case-Based Analysis of Design Features for Decision Quality and Process Traceability
affiliations: DHBW Mannheim

detail.title: Governing Agentic AI in Finance: A Use-Case-Based Analysis of Design Features for Decision Quality and Process Traceability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The classification of information, the derivation of action decisions from such classifications, and their automated execution represent central challenges in the financial sector. Agentic AI systems offer a promising approach to automating such tasks. However, given the potential consequences of erroneous decisions, minimizing misclassification risk, ensuring decision traceability, and maintaining process consistency are essential prerequisites for deploying this technology. This paper introduces the key concepts of agentic AI, presents an automated portfolio risk-alert system as a practical use case, and examines three system designs that differ with respect to their degree of process autonomy and structural design choices. Using a design science research approach, we derive transferable design principles that increase decision quality as well as decision process traceability and consistency, which are transferable to other use cases for information processing and decision making in finance. The designs are moreover empirically tested across twelve example cases and twenty repeated runs each. The results suggest that restricting process autonomy leads to more consistent process paths and a higher share of correct risk assessments. Furthermore, requiring structured LLM outputs and storing intermediate results in a structured manner substantially increases the traceability of information assessments and decisions.

detail.abstract: This article audits the Competition Authority of Kenya from 2012 to 2025, reading its annual reports closely against the Economic Surveys, case law and scholarship. It credits real achievements: fast merger review, a major cartel penalty confirmed on appeal, a distinctive buyer-power doctrine and a surging consumer docket. It then exposes persistent gaps between penalties announced and booked, complaints received and finalized, and mandate and means. The article argues that the Authority practices throughput regulation, rewarding volume over market outcomes. It proposes a three-ledger test and seven practical reforms on funding, concurrency, digital markets, informality, regional notification and outcome measurement.

title: The Liquidity Lifecycle of Tokenized Assets: A Dynamic Theory of Secondary Market Transitions
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney

detail.title: The Liquidity Lifecycle of Tokenized Assets: A Dynamic Theory of Secondary Market Transitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: This research is funded by the Digital Finance CRC, supported by the Cooperative Research Centres Program, an Australian Government initiative.

detail.abstract: Tokenized real-world assets consistently suffer from persistent secondary market illiquidity, challenging the crypto-native assumption that market microstructure evolves along a linear trajectory from constant product automated market makers (CPMMs) to concentrated liquidity (CL-AMMs) and central limit order books (CLOBs). We develop a continuous-time microstructural model demonstrating that for assets subject to discrete valuation audits, this evolutionary logic is fundamentally inverted. Bootstrapping on continuous invariant curves triggers immediate adverse selection and prohibitive balance-sheet carry. Instead, the asset must incubate on a discrete Issuer-Gated Request-for-Quote (RFQ) to eliminate latency arbitrage, deploy the CL-AMM as an intermediate algorithmic buffer during market adolescence, and converge on an endogenous dual-venue terminal equilibrium. As secondary turnover systematically compresses valuation uncertainty, discretionary market flow migrates to a capital-efficient continuous CLOB, while a fractional allocation is retained on an issuer-subsidized CPMM to guarantee atomic on-chain composability. Finally, we formalize the Mega-Cap Paradox, proving that invariant curves face an absolute balance-sheet capacity limit that precludes monolithic automated liquidity for institutional-grade funds.

detail.abstract: The expansion of dual-channel supply chains has intensified manufacturer-retailer competition, while carbon-cost internalization increasingly affects firms' pricing, service, and channel decisions. This study develops a Stackelberg framework under a no-free-allowance carbon-cost regime to examine retailer service enhancement and manufacturer encroachment across different channel configurations. Three settings are considered, namely retailer service enhancement without manufacturer encroachment (NS), manufacturer encroachment without retailer service enhancement (ED), and a no-service, no-encroachment benchmark (ND). The analysis yields three main findings. First, demand-side characteristics shape the viability and profitability of the two strategic responses. Greater sensitivity to service enhancement increases both firms' equilibrium profits under NS, whereas greater DTC acceptance expands the conditions under which manufacturer encroachment can remain active under ED. Second, carbon-cost internalization affects the viability of the two strategies through different mechanisms. The NS model remains economically viable only when the aggregate carbon burden is sufficiently low, whereas the viability of active DTC operation under ED depends jointly on the DTC operating cost, consumer acceptance, and firm-specific carbon burdens. Third, carbon-cost pressure is allocated differently across channel structures. Under NS, the carbon burdens of both firms accumulate through the retail channel, whereas active ED reallocates these burdens through wholesale pricing, DTC pricing, and demand allocation. Managerially, manufacturers should support DTC viability by controlling direct-channel operating costs and emission intensity, while retailers should strengthen service effectiveness and both firms should coordinate emission-reduction efforts to preserve market viability under increasing carbon-cost pressure.

title: Chinese Belt and Road Infrastructure Investments and Sri Lanka's Tourism Resilience: A Qualitative Content Analysis of Strategic Megaprojects

detail.abstract: This study aims to assess how the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative infrastructure development projects influence tourism resilience and destination adaptability in Sri Lanka. In the context of multiple macroeconomic shocks and crises, tourism economies are capitalizing on infrastructure as a key production factor. The research explores the impact of transportation, maritime, and urban infrastructure development on tourism through a qualitative content analysis of selected secondary sources. The analyzed data includes Central Bank reports, Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority strategy research, policy, and documents from 2015-2026, and China-Sri Lanka bilateral development agreements. The study is inspired by the Resource-Based View and Institutional Theory and identifies three tourism destination resilience factors: improved transportation and connectivity, tourism product diversification, and institutional stability and long-term capital investment. The research finds that infrastructure resilience serves as a critical sustainability factor for tourism destinations in Sri Lanka. The findings also show that specific infrastructure assets can generate substantial tourism value and counterbalance multiple economic shocks by creating new transportation routes, diversifying tourism products, and institutionalizing long-term capital investment. This study contributes to the discussion on macroeconomic sustainability factors by advancing the Resource-Based View theory to mega-project level infrastructure assets. The findings may be useful to policymakers and tourism planners in Sri Lanka and the global south to capitalize on large-scale infrastructure investments to develop tourism economies.

title: Optimization-Consistent Drawdown-Capital Attribution
affiliations: Renmin University of China

detail.title: Optimization-Consistent Drawdown-Capital Attribution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Traditional performance attribution explains where return came from, while portfolio optimization decides whether the capital assigned to each strategy remains economically justified. These functions use different mathematical objects: attribution is additive and retrospective, whereas reallocation is marginal and forward-looking. This paper develops a unified drawdown-capital framework that keeps the two roles distinct but links them through the same economic capital functional. Marginal drawdown-capital cost is the shadow cost of expanding a strategy. A path-integrated allocation, defined as an Aumann-Shapley line integral from the zero portfolio to the observed portfolio, is exactly additive even when the capital penalty is nonlinear and current marginal cost times position is not. Constrained first-order conditions decompose expected return into compensation for drawdown capital and rents created by binding limits. The Attribution Improvement Score, Sᵢ = ∂G/∂wᵢ − ρ ∂C/∂wᵢ, is the gradient numerator of portfolio efficiency ρ = G / C. It gives a first-order rule for feasible transfers, remains meaningful when marginal drawdown cost is zero or negative, and connects directly to three policies: maximize expected return at a fixed capital budget, minimize capital at a fixed expected return, or maximize the efficiency ratio through fractional programming. A unified five-strategy calibration shows why current marginal allocations can overstate nonlinear economic capital and how the score identifies portfolio-improving directions. A rolling public-fund sleeve application using 2020Q1 exposure groups and 2022Q2-2025Q4 out-of-sample returns provides a realistic data exercise. Over fifteen out-of-sample quarters all three attribution-guided policies reduce annualized volatility from 14.72% to between 11.58% and 12.15%, and maximum drawdown from 22.12% to between 16.73% and 18.54%, at annualized returns of 3.21% to 3.72% against the benchmark 3.45%. The finding is risk reduction at comparable return rather than return enhancement, and it holds under all three governance objectives rather than resting on one. The application is illustrative rather than hedge-fund causal evidence, but it demonstrates how the same attribution engine can be estimated, constrained, and evaluated out of sample.

detail.abstract: The paper proposes a functional forecasting framework for the next-day path of spot betas. We reconstruct spot betas from asynchronously sampled transaction prices using Fourier estimators of spot covariance and variance. Motivated by the empirical features of spot beta estimates, we employ robust dynamic functional principal component analysis for dimension reduction and forecast the resulting scores using autoregressive models, residual networks and cross-sectional elastic pooling. Using 30 largecap NASDAQ-listed stocks over 2022-2024, we find that score-based models outperform forecasting benchmarks, including functional autoregression. Pooling improves upon stock-specific autoregressive models, while adding a residual network under full pooling yields no significant further gain. By contrast, elastic pooling significantly outperforms the fully pooled autoregression, both with and without residual network augmentation. As a complementary contribution, we derive a stable central limit theorem for the spot beta estimator employed and a feasible closed-form rule for selecting the Fourier cutoff frequencies, thereby providing a fully operational procedure for obtaining the spot beta estimates that feed the forecasting exercise.

detail.abstract: Much has been written about technology and AI altering how diplomats communicate and relate. Scholarly and practitioner concern in this context has often centred on how diplomacy's legacy institutions might adapt to, or be updated in the face of, technological change. This is the focus of a burgeoning field of international relations scholarship and practice surrounding so-called 'tech diplomacy'. This article argues for a different approach in and to this field: not for the making technological of diplomacy so much as the making diplomatic of conflicts arising from the growing ubiquity of AI and the rising power of a relatively small number of dominant tech players across the global landscape. It argues for the potential value of framing human-nonhuman relations in this context as diplomatic problems and approaching these in combination with other dilemmas of human-nonhuman interface in the Anthropocene, drawing upon recent work in the humanities that casts "diplomacy" in a heterodox register.

detail.abstract: Resale is often promoted as a remedy for fashion overproduction. Yet evidence indicates that fashion resale may stimulate additional consumption, potentially offsetting the new purchases it displaces. Whether and under what conditions these opposing forces yield a net reduction in fashion production remains unresolved. We analyze these questions by incorporating consumers' desire for variety, a distinctive feature of fashion consumption, into the classical framework of durable goods resale. We show that a frictionless resale market-which can reduce production but may fail to clear for durable goods-always clears but increases production for fashion goods. Variety-seeking thus shifts the central challenge from sustaining resale trade to containing the production increase it stimulates. Transaction frictions, conventionally viewed as barriers to circularity, can instead enable fashion resale to reduce production. This reversal provides an environmental rationale for service-oriented resale intermediation, in which meaningful commissions both generate revenue and temper consumption expansion. Independent third-party resale platforms are better positioned to maintain this service orientation, whereas brand-operated platforms may depart from it by sacrificing commission revenue to stimulate new sales, a misalignment intensified by competition. Extended Producer Responsibility can realign brands' incentives through post-use treatment fees on new products, whereas eco-modulating these fees to reward resale can inadvertently exacerbate production. Our results suggest that whether fashion resale curbs overproduction depends on how it is operated. Realizing resale's environmental potential calls for a shift in business models and policies from expanding transactions toward developing profitable resale services that decouple the fashion industry's revenue from virgin production.

detail.abstract:
Cambodia’s digital economy has transformed substantially over the past decade, yet empirical evidence documenting the formative stage of e-business adoption remains limited. This study revisits original research conducted in Cambodia in 2016 to examine the technological, market, transactional, and institutional conditions that shaped e-business adoption during an early stage of the country’s digital transformation.

The original study employed a structured online survey administered through SurveyMonkey from 31 July to 29 August 2016, generating 200 responses. The survey was supplemented by contemporaneous evidence concerning internet and mobile connectivity, digital platforms, payment infrastructure, regulation, and Cambodia’s emerging e-commerce environment. It also incorporated an applied organizational case involving Business Khmer, an early Cambodian digital-content venture that was subsequently rebranded as BizKhmer and developed into BizKhmer Digital Media Co., Ltd. The later organizational trajectory is used as a retrospective illustration of enterprise adaptation rather than as longitudinal causal evidence.

The historical evidence reveals a central paradox of early-stage digitalization: expanding connectivity created access to online markets without necessarily creating equivalent readiness to transact within them. Although respondents demonstrated substantial exposure to local online platforms and optimism regarding the future of e-commerce, significant barriers remained. Payment-method problems were identified by 64.10% of respondents, followed by security concerns (54.36%), lack of trust (50.77%), and low consumer awareness (37.95%). Respondents most frequently recommended easy and trusted payment mechanisms (74.24%) and stronger trust-building measures (64.65%) as priorities for promoting e-commerce. These findings indicate that connectivity alone was insufficient to generate mature e-business adoption when consumer confidence, payment mechanisms, market capabilities, and supporting institutions remained under development.

Building on the historical evidence and established technology-adoption literature, the paper develops an Emerging-Economy E-Business Adoption Framework (EEBAF) comprising four complementary dimensions: digital infrastructure, consumer and market readiness, transactional readiness, and the institutional environment. EEBAF conceptualizes e-business adoption as an ecosystem-level process in which technological connectivity enables participation, while sustained adoption depends on complementary development across market, transactional, and institutional conditions.

The paper further uses post-2016 evidence to contextualize Cambodia’s subsequent development in digital payments, e-commerce regulation, platform-based commerce, and MSME digitalization while maintaining a clear distinction between the original 2016 findings and retrospective interpretation. The study contributes historically grounded evidence from Cambodia’s early digital economy, proposes EEBAF as a framework for understanding e-business adoption in emerging economies, and advances a central proposition: digital connectivity creates the opportunity for e-business, but ecosystem readiness determines whether that opportunity develops into trusted, repeatable, and scalable digital economic activity. The paper concludes with propositions for future empirical testing of EEBAF in Cambodia and other emerging economies.

Keywords: E-Business; E-Commerce; Digital Economy; Cambodia; Emerging Economies; Digital Adoption; Digital Infrastructure; Consumer Trust; Digital Payments; Market Readiness; Transactional Readiness; Institutional Environment; MSMEs; Digital Entrepreneurship; Southeast Asia

detail.abstract:
The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence in legal practice has produced a nationwide surge in judicial sanctions, most prominently for the submission of fabricated legal authorities. This Article presents what is, so far as the author has been able to determine as of August 2026, the first comprehensive survey of judicial responses to AI-assisted legal misconduct, analyzing over one hundred sanctions decisions issued between 2023 and 2026 across more than sixty federal and state jurisdictions, supplemented by empirical analysis of a database cataloging 789 entries of AI-related misconduct in American courts. It traces the evolution of courts’ approaches from early educational warnings to sophisticated detection methods, standardized sanctions, and prophylactic rules requiring disclosure and verification of AI use.

Across jurisdictions, courts uniformly reject any “AI exception” to professional responsibility. Applying existing frameworks—principally Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 and Model Rules of Professional Conduct 1.1, 3.3, and 5.1—courts hold that the duty to verify legal authority is nondelegable and that conscious avoidance of verification constitutes bad faith. The empirical data reveal a hierarchy of harm keyed not to the filer’s culpability but to the object of the fabrication, which the Article proposes that courts adopt explicitly as a three-tiered framework: Tier One, Fabricated Authority; Tier Two, Fabricated Record; Tier Three, Fabricated Reality. No court or commentator appears previously to have organized AI-related misconduct along that axis or to have tested the ordering against sanction outcomes. Courts already sanction along the gradient—the median monetary sanction for fabricating the record is $5,600 against $1,485 for fabricating authority—and a second divide separates represented from unrepresented filers: attorneys lose filings, pro se litigants lose cases. Synthesizing sanctionable conduct, rationales, and severity factors, the Article demonstrates a clear national consensus: AI may assist lawyers, but it does not diminish professional responsibility, and failure to verify AI-generated work now carries predictable, escalating, and nationwide consequences.

detail.abstract: We demonstrate that book-tax differences (BTD), a measure commonly used in accounting research, may result in an OLS regression coefficient that is difficult to interpret. Because the two components that make up BTD—accounting income and taxable income—are combined into a single regression variable, the resulting coefficient is constrained and can differ from the coefficients that would result if the two components were included as separate regression variables. We illustrate this econometric issue by providing theoretical derivations, replicating prior empirical studies, and showing how the constrained coefficient on BTD can mask the underlying relationships between each component and the variable of interest. We survey published studies to document how frequently BTD is used in published research and suggest diagnostics for researchers who use BTD.

detail.abstract:
Secular cycles, oscillations of political instability with periods of one to three centuries, are a central claim of structural-demographic theory and the target of the Koopman programme of this series (WP-2026-005, WP-2026-006). Before a historical test can be read, one must know whether it could have seen a cycle if there were one. We answer this question in vitro. We plant a slow cycle of known period and coherence in simulated societies, and we measure the power of a size-calibrated pooled Hankel-DMD test against a null twin without the cycle. We also measure the forecast value of the detected cycle for crisis onsets 10 to 200 years ahead. The design, the hypotheses and the decision rules were preregistered, and the verification was run once on fresh seeds. For a 200-year cycle with coherence time three periods and moderate observation noise, observed at decadal cadence with a 70-year delay window, power 0.8 needs about 350-390 pooled decadal columns, however they are split between societies and years: 32 × 200 years, 8 × 500, 4 × 1,000 or 2 × 2,000. The strict historical panel of independent states since 1789 sits at the edge, with power 0.79 [0.73, 0.84] (a post hoc interval; the preregistered rule counts detections, §6). A noisy proxy of the slow driver lifts it to 1.00. The persistence criterion used in WP-2026-006 has power at most 0.07 on its own premise. Once detected, the cycle's phase beats a renewal model by 0.16 of Brier skill at 100 years, as preregistered; in an exploratory comparison it falls short of a hazard model on the observed state, which keeps positive skill up to 200 years. In vitro, long-horizon skill comes from the observed state and the model class, not from spectral detection as such.

detail.abstract: By raising the share of life spent in retirement, demographic aging shortens the duration of individuals' labor earnings relative to their consumption horizons. Since labor income is relatively safe, its shortening duration increases households' desire for safe bonds and lowers their capacity to bear equity risk. Slower population growth reinforces these effects. A consequence of aging is therefore a lower safe rate, with the risk premium rising to make aging investors willing to absorb the risk. In a two-country model in which Foreign ages more severely, Home households (which we identify with the U.S.) optimally supply safe bonds and take leveraged equity positions, as they are in the better relative position to do so. As a result, Home's equity premium rises by more than Foreign's, consistent with the evidence. Quantitatively, we find that demographic changes since 1980 have lowered the world safe rate by 71 basis points and raised the U.S. equity premium by 251 basis points (compared with 49 basis points abroad). Aging can therefore lower safe returns globally while raising the compensation required to bear equity risk - particularly in the "younger" country, which is better placed to absorb such risk and becomes the global safe asset issuer.

detail.abstract: We consider testing equality of means and recovering homogeneous clusters in a growing number of independent populations. We propose an ordered adaptive fusion procedure that penalizes consecutive differences between empirical means after ordering. The procedure recovers equality among population means without imposing sparsity on their levels. Under the global equality hypothesis, all populations are fused with probability tending to one. Under alternatives, the true partition into homogeneous populations is also recovered with probability tending to one, while the estimated common means have the same first-order distribution as the corresponding oracle estimators. Thus, testing, cluster recovery and estimation are obtained within a single framework when the number of populations diverges.

detail.abstract: Changes in credit spreads are not the only way in which financial markets adjust to shocks in investor and bank lending capacity. Firms can also respond by changing the composition of debt claims they issue across instruments and markets. We measure the price-elasticity of substitution of corporate debt supply in primary markets. Using granular data on syndicated loans and corporate bonds issued by firms worldwide, we exploit variation in borrowing costs driven by shifts in bank lending capacity and institutional demand for bonds to estimate three margins of debt supply: substitution across instruments within a market, substitution between bank and bond financing, and the scale of total debt issuance. We find that firms respond elastically along all three margins. Therefore, the composition of corporate debt supply is a key channel through which financial markets adjust to shocks in investor and bank lending capacity.

detail.abstract: This study examines performance persistence among worldwide short-term fixedincome mutual funds. This research examines a sample of 19,459 fixed-income mutual funds around the world during the period 1990-2025. Performance is measured using an index derived from the Sharpe ratio but designed to resolve certain issues that can arise with the latter. The analysis of persistence employs a contingency table methodology, while Malkiel's (1995) statistic is used to assess the robustness of the persistence phenomenon. Finally, the practical value of understanding this persistence phenomenon is empirically demonstrated.

detail.abstract: Crypto gains can be hidden in self-custodied or offshore wallets, but crypto losses are claimed by taxpayers and verified. We show that this asymmetry ties the optimal crypto gains tax to loss relief and enforcement. In a two-asset model with private crypto services, external effects, costly concealment and costly detection, a higher statutory rate raises investors' tax burden only if the detection probability exceeds the share of expected gains returned as loss credits, ℓ c L c /G c. Below that threshold, a rate increase subsidizes crypto holdings and loses revenue. Under imperfect collection, limiting loss relief while lowering the rate implements the same allocation with less concealment and more revenue. The enforcement cost of loss relief disappears as third-party reporting becomes complete. In a calibration matched to evidence on crypto compliance, return dispersion, and holdings, the detection threshold is 0.57. With costless full reporting, the optimal crypto rate is 25 percent against a 20 percent equity rate. With imperfect collection, it falls to about 4 percent, and removing loss relief raises welfare. Bringing self-custodied holdings under third-party reporting raises the optimal rate to 16-20 percent.

detail.abstract: The Shapley correspondence for non-transferable-utility games can assign several allocations to the same cooperative economy. This paper establishes a global restriction on those solutions. For games with finite coalition supports on the nonnegative cone satisfying stated smoothness and boundary-entry conditions, the normalized comparison equations have topological degree (-1) n-1. When all solutions are regular, their indices obey a signed-count identity and the number of comparison solutions is odd. If distinct comparison solutions yield distinct payoffs, the allocation count is also odd. Under stronger support smoothness, regularity is generic, and individual regular solutions persist under small changes in coalition opportunities. These restrictions coexist with substantial indeterminacy: for every n ≥ 3, we construct superadditive games with finite, entirely regular correspondences containing at least 2 ⌊n/3⌋ + 1 distinct allocations. The global index also provides a necessary check on numerical enumeration: a certified list of regular solutions whose index sum differs from the global degree is incomplete, while agreement alone does not establish completeness.

detail.abstract: Cross-fund subscriptions and redemptions are a growing feature of the investment fund landscape, with direct implications for funding stability and the transmission of liquidity risk. Using highly granular central bank statistical data on German open-ended funds, I document that these cross-fund flows create a funding-side network that actively channels liquidity between funds. I find that these direct fund-to-fund flows can (i) substantially exceed funds' cash buffers, (ii) provide partial liquidity insurance by absorbing idiosyncratic shocks, but also transmit and amplify funding pressure across the network, especially during systemic liquidity distress episodes, and (iii) interact with monetary policy, as tightening prompts funds to build up cash and withdraw liquidity from the network. Funds held by other funds are particularly fragile, facing elevated downside flow risk. Overall, cross-fund flows represent a new and significant channel through which liquidity shortages and surpluses propagate in non-bank financial networks.

detail.abstract: The erosion of planetary stability-the network of environmental, cultural, economic, and political systems that sustain prosperity-by human-induced environmental change has activated scientific, social, and political collective actions worldwide. Here, I suggest that a realistic threat to humanity is not posed by this or any single disruptive phenomenon, but by the synergies among the five greatest modern threats: environmental change, erosion of democracy, of peace, and of rigorous information, and artificial intelligence. These threats have outpaced institutional responses to regulate their detrimental impacts, progressively dragging humanity towards a regime of natural selection whereby civilisations risks normalising the 'strongest' 'predating' over the rest. I argue that institutional regulation (global, national) of threats and unrestrained power is the only viable future for humanity.

detail.abstract: Individual stock-return forecasting is inherently a low signal-to-noise problem. This reality has led to forecast evaluations in which the zero forecast is routinely used as a benchmark. We document that this benchmark is excessively conservative. Outperforming the zero forecast, in fact, may simply reflect ability to predict level effects, i.e., changes in the market return or market-timing, rather than cross-sectional dispersion. Consistent with this observation, we document that the panel historical mean provides a more stringent and informative benchmark. The panel historical mean is economically interpretable as the historical mean return of the market portfolio and is nested within standard machine-learning models as the limiting case in which firm characteristics have no predictive role. We formalize the difficulty of outperforming this new benchmark through a finite-sample analysis of Ridge in a low signal-to-noise environment. Relative to the panel historical mean, only flexible nonlinear models generate consistent predictive gains, which are - however - concentrated among small, value, and illiquid stocks.

detail.abstract: Weekend work is a pervasive feature of labor markets that comes with both potential benefits (e.g., higher pay, flexible schedules) and drawbacks (e.g., less social time). Nevertheless, robust evidence on weekend workers’ job satisfaction is lacking. Longitudinal data from 21 waves of the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey (n=211,077; i=26,273) are used to estimate the association between weekend work and several dimensions of job satisfaction. Estimates from fixed effects models reveal that weekend work is associated with significantly lower levels of satisfaction with working hours and flexibility, but this does not translate into lower levels of overall job satisfaction. Additional analyses were conducted to test whether results varied with employment status, occupation and parental status. In general, the main finding applied to all groups examined. There were, however, marked differences across sub-groups in satisfaction with other job domains. Overall, the results suggest that, for most workers, the benefits of working weekends offset its disadvantages.

detail.abstract: A dictionary counts words; a large language model (LLM) reads them in context. I ask whether that difference reduces the information frictions that keep textual disclosure out of prices. Scoring default likelihood from earnings call transcripts, and putting both readers on identical text, I find that it does, and does so where interpretation is contested. The score forecasts rating migration a year ahead; what the dictionary sees is already in the spread quoted at the call, and what the LLM sees is not. Where analysts disagreed, the score forecasts bond returns for one to two weeks; where they agreed, it does not. It does not explain post-earnings announcement drift, which concentrates where bonds are costly to trade rather than where calls are hard to read. What an LLM reads from a call is real, is priced, and is sometimes priced late; it is not what the drift is made of.

detail.abstract:
Firm-level environmental research needs geographic measurements whose interpretation remains consistent across locations and years. Linking company addresses to ecological rasters introduces choices about coordinate reference, spatial support and missingness that can alter company-year values. We audit an existing office-location linkage for Chinese listed companies. The recovered panel contains 49,022 unique firm-years for 5,302 firms during 2007–2022. Complete file-size and MD5 comparisons identify all 16 annual inputs as CFATD Parts III–VI. The original producer averages angular-grid squares and retains numeric zeros; every joined coordinate is unchanged from the geocoding output. Fresh extraction reproduces all point values and three square means/counts on a preserved 200-point-year sample, with means agreeing exactly after four-decimal serialization. Point values are zero in 88.41% of the panel, compared with 0.57% for the middle-square mean. In pooled average-tie ranks, 33.05% of observations move by more than ten percentile points between narrower and middle squares, and 52.83% between wider and middle squares. These findings establish numerical reproducibility and substantial stored-support sensitivity. Coordinate and ecological mask interpretation remain unresolved. The contribution is an auditable measurement workflow with shared software, methods and aggregate results; real observations remain private. The audit does not establish metric buffer distances, ecological absence, biodiversity risk or corporate impact.

detail.abstract:
Two simple rules are widely used to limit drawdowns in equity portfolios. The 200-day moving-average rule moves to cash when the price closes below its trailing 200-day average; volatility targeting scales the position by the ratio of a long-run to a recent estimate of volatility. We compare the two, and their combination, in a registered walk-forward test on SPY from 2000 to 2025 and on thirteen other exchange-traded funds. Each rule has one setting fixed in advance, positions never exceed full investment, and every trade costs 0.02%.
We sort SPY's six drawdowns of 15% or more by speed. In the prolonged bear markets of 2000 to 2002 and 2007 to 2009 the moving-average rule lost less than half as much as SPY and recovered years earlier; volatility targeting cut the 2007 to 2009 loss by a third but did not help in 2000 to 2002. In the fast crashes of 2018 and 2020 volatility targeting lost about as much as the moving-average rule or less and recovered months earlier. Over the full period volatility targeting compounded at 6.28% a year against 6.12% for SPY, while the moving-average rule gave up 1.67 points a year, partly through repeated exits and re-entries in trendless markets. Sorting the events by speed tells which rule protected better in four of the six; which rule acted first depended instead on how sharply volatility rose.

detail.abstract: Strong demand provides special opportunities for developing countries with critical minerals to negotiate beneficial contracts with international investors; but also, it poses special risks. For example, skilled negotiators can exploit the eagerness of investors’ home country governments to secure supplies by insisting that they contribute to development. On the other hand, changing technology and investors’ drive for safety of supply can lead to agreements that tie up resources without ever generating actual production and benefits. To get the best possible deal by grasping opportunities and protecting against certain risks, many countries can benefit from pro bono negotiation assistance offered by organizations such as the CONNEX Support Unit, ISLP and the ALSF.

title: How about flies? Economic behavior of connectome-derived agents
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: How about flies? Economic behavior of connectome-derived agents
detail.abstract: The paper studies software agents built from a 2,000-neuron subgraph of MaleCNS, a reconstructed map of a male fruit fly’s neural connections. The agents face Holt–Laury lotteries, the Allais paradox and a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma, with published human experiments providing the benchmarks. They make fewer safe lottery choices than humans—4.125 against 5.2—yet all 24 primary controllers exhibit the conventional Allais reversal. In repeated interaction, cooperation averages approximately 38% and declines with experience. The agents respond to a reciprocal opponent but fail to reproduce humans’ high initial cooperation followed by terminal defection in later matches. Control treatments show that changes in neural connections, payoff representation and learning speed affect the agents’ choices. Simulated flies thus offer a complementary class of experimental subjects for studying preferences and strategic behavior.

detail.abstract: I estimate own-price elasticities and cross-brand substitution across two differentiated formats-whey powders and protein bars-using a Berry (1994) nested logit estimated by Berry inversion with cluster-robust OLS on 861 product-flavour SKUs (157 products, 11 flavour markets), validated against a 274-week promotional panel. detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of sectoral heterogeneity on fiscal multipliers in China, focusing on resource reallocation between the capital-intensive heavy sector and the laborintensive light sector. By applying a Bayesian SVAR model to identify fiscal spending shocks over 1992Q1-2015Q3, we find an aggregate output multiplier of 0.76, with output multipliers of 1.09 for the heavy sector and-0.25 for the light sector. Fiscal spending shocks lead to rising labor costs, declining capital costs, and the disappearance of light-sector firms-all driven by factor reallocation. Our two-sector model with heterogeneous producers and financial frictions explains these dynamics, highlighting the role of fiscal policy in reshaping sectoral outputs.

detail.abstract: Experts detect asset bubbles with econometric tests; ordinary investors only have headlines on the news. This paper asks whether the structural state of a bubble can be captured in one simple, transparent number that a non-specialist can compute from free public data. The Bubble Intensity Score (BIS) is the equal-weighted mean of four pillar z-scores: valuation, leverage, sentiment and concentration, each measured against its own trailing ten-year history. Backtested against pre-registered criteria, the index peaked at +2.20 in February 2000, one month before the Nasdaq's top, after first warning in July 1999, demonstrating that the pillar decomposition holds true for past financial bubbles. Applied to the AI-era market, the index reads +0.78 (June 2026): valuation comparable to December 1999, concentration elevated, but leverage at its decade average and sentiment negative; similar to the year 1999, but not fragile like 2007's, implying correction risk rather than systemic collapse.

title: Instrumentalized Innocence: Child Financial Exploitation, Caregiver Dependency, and the Limits of the U.S. Child Protection Framework
affiliations: Intenovate Inc.

detail.title: Instrumentalized Innocence: Child Financial Exploitation, Caregiver Dependency, and the Limits of the U.S. Child Protection Framework

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Child financial exploitation can occur when a minor’s identity, labor, earnings, assets, economic rights, or economic dependency are used to produce financial or material benefit for another person under circumstances that compromise the child’s interests, agency, or developmental position. Existing U.S. legal and institutional frameworks address components of this conduct through child-protection, consumer, labor, property, criminal, forced-labor, and emerging digital-content law, leaving economically related harms distributed across systems with different jurisdictional and evidentiary requirements.

This article develops child financial exploitation as an analytical category and examines four principal modalities: identity-based financial exploitation; exploitative participation in caregiver- or family-controlled enterprises; extraction of children’s earnings and assets; and psychological coercion associated with economic compliance. It further examines monetized digital content as an expanding setting in which children’s labor, identities, likenesses, and private lives can generate economic value under adult control.

Drawing on primary legal authority and interdisciplinary peer-reviewed scholarship, the analysis considers how developmental dependency, economic control, allocation of benefit and burden, meaningful choice, and coercion distinguish potentially exploitative conduct from ordinary family economic interdependence. It also examines the structural relationship between child financial exploitation and forced-labor law while preserving the statutory requirements necessary to establish a federal trafficking offense.

The article develops a six-dimensional framework for practitioner inquiry encompassing the economic resource involved, control over that resource, allocation of benefit, allocation of burden, meaningful choice and coercion, and developmental and legal context. It maps corresponding responses across child protection, consumer protection, labor regulation, property and trust law, criminal law, and state protections for minors participating in monetized digital content. The analysis concludes that economic harms originating during childhood can persist beyond the jurisdictional boundaries of child-protection systems and proposes a coordinated reform agenda centered on recognition, referral, prevention, economic remedies, and empirical evaluation. Economic autonomy emerges as a significant component of the transition from child protection to independent adulthood.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how drug trafficking and public corruption interact to impede capital accumulation and economic development. In an overlapping generations model, an illegal firm sells drugs to workers and bribes bureaucrats to overlook its activities. Workers who consume drugs face a risk of premature death and therefore do not save. We demonstrate that multiple steady states exist: a high-capital steady state without drug trafficking or corruption, characterized by high welfare, and a low-capital poverty trap where both are prevalent. Escaping the trap is challenging because the policies that could eliminate it-stronger monitoring and penalties, along with tax cuts-make the current generation of bureaucrats worse off and are therefore not Pareto-improving. By contrast, a sufficiently large improvement in technology diminishes the profitability of drug trafficking. It expands the tax base that funds bureaucrats' salaries, providing a Pareto-improving exit from the poverty trap. This finding suggests that, given the political and fiscal constraints on domestic policies, technology transfer from abroad, such as official development assistance, can substantially contribute to economic development.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an autonomous research loop in which large language model (LLM) agents build a multi-factor equity alpha model from start to finish, while a fixed, rule-based harness keeps every step auditable. Agents decide what to test, and code decides how it is measured. A runner model (Claude Opus) executes the search from a standing instruction file, an advisor model (Claude Fable) reviews phase boundaries and acceptances, and five sub-agents with restricted tools fetch, verify, translate, audit and evaluate each predictor in Chen and Zimmermann's (2022) Open Source Asset Pricing catalogue on a frozen Sharadar dataset. The acceptance bars, a long-short ranked within sector and hedged to the market by an ex-ante beta, and a 57-month out-of-sample period were fixed before any candidate was screened, and the human answers a closed list of seven questions rather than directing the search. The loop inventoried all 212 catalogue predictors in Chen and Zimmermann (2022), screened the 107 the data could construct, and admitted 14 whose information was significant beyond every leg already held, raising a Fama-French (2015) plus-momentum baseline's mean rank IC from 0.0145 to 0.0389 over 1999 to 2021. Out of sample the IC held at 0.0300, while the hedged long-short earned about half its expected Sharpe (0.523 against 0.996), most of it from the hedge term. The contribution is the framework rather than the model: a research process that runs itself, traces every number to the data and code that produced it, and reports a mixed result against expectations it wrote down before it looked.

detail.abstract: Between 1809 and 1811, American shipping through the Danish Sound recovered to 86 per cent of its 1806 peak (168 passages in 1811 against 195 in 1806), but the recovery transformed what the trade carried. Drawing on 2,378 certain-tier American passages from the Sound Toll Registers (STRO), this article shows that the American outbound leg became a majority of the route: United States-to-Europe passages, including 47 American-origin voyages declaring only Østersøen (Baltic region), rose from 19.0 to 51.5 per cent of the total between 1801-1806 and 1809-1811. Within the merged outbound leg, dyewoods rose from 24.6 to 72.1 per cent of passages (4.3 to 26.8 per cent excluding the disputed Stokf. holt reading), and cotton, on 3.5 per cent of baseline passages, appeared on 72.7 per cent of outbound and 41.1 per cent of all recovery-period passages. The Sound series is a filtered sample: Danish enforcement after 1807 selected which vessels dared the passage, so counts are lower bounds on the underlying trade. Captain turnover matched the peacetime baseline under strict and fuzzy matching alike; round-trip completion fell from 34.3 to 13.4 per cent of eastbound captains, consistent with a shift from triangular to direct wartime sailings.

detail.abstract: Alfred W. Crosby's America, Russia, Hemp, and Napoleon (1965) measured American trade with Russia and the Baltic from the departure end. This article measures the same trade from the transit end: the Danish Sound toll registers (STRO 2.0), passage by passage, 1783-1815. American passages are identified through the captain's domicile in a three-tier classification (2,551 certain passages). Traffic rose from 3 passages in 1783 to a prewar peak of 195 in 1806. No American-domiciled passages are recorded in 1807; the absence is domicileselective (Danish domiciles 607 to zero, American 192 to zero, British undiminished) and cannot be read as a measured trade stop. The 1809-1811 neutral-carrier boom recovered to 86 per cent of the prewar peak by 1811 (49, 138 and 168 passages) and changed the outbound leg in kind: American domestic produce rebounded past its earlier level while reexported dyewoods, expanding from 23.7 per cent of outbound passages in 1801-1808, rose to three-quarters of direct sailings with stated destinations (101 of 136), St. Petersburg holding as the hub. Outbound holds were mixed: 81 of 136 carried both domestic produce and dyewoods. On the value side, the eighty-six-fold rise of US exports to Russia between 1805 and 1811 is substantially a clearance-destination artefact: merging the Russia and Denmark-Norway series cuts 1805-1810 growth from 55.7-fold to 7.3-fold (9.9-fold adding Sweden via a proxy).

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to explain why Kenya guarantees academic freedom and still rations it. It traces the Kenyan academy from the 1970s to 2026 through law, history and sociology. Two case studies anchor the argument. They examine the literature department and the law faculty at the University of Nairobi. The paper shows how the Moi state infiltrated universities. Informers, permits, passports and a loyalty curriculum were its instruments. It then follows the same logic into the multiparty era. There markets and appointments replaced detention. The argument is that Kenya practices custodial autonomy. Freedom is declared on paper yet kept in executive custody. Three hands of control emerge: the heavy, the invisible and the procedural. Each hand borrowed its instruments from the one before. Each era is traced through documents, testimony and doctrine. Article 33(1)(c) of the 2010 Constitution appears as a promise without a guardian. The paper tests that promise against the Universities Act 2012, litigation and digital regulation. It closes with reforms for statute, institutions, courts and scholars. It also invites further debate on constitutional text and institutional courage.

detail.abstract: The ship Empress of China opened direct American trade with China in 1784. This article asks whether the men who commanded the early China voyages came from the Revolutionary War's maritime world, and develops a reproducible method for answering that question from digitized ship news. From 5,996 pages of Library of Congress newspapers (1784-1800), I extract 242 voyage records naming 132 merged captains and match them against a systematic roster of 1,129 Revolutionary War privateer captains (from 1,615 letter-of-marque bonds) and a published roster of 178 Continental Navy officers. Five individuals satisfy a rule requiring both a roster hit and independent biographical confirmation — the privateersmen Thomas Truxtun and James Magee, and the naval officers John Barry, Thomas Read, and Richard Dale — at 23 of 242 voyage mentions (9.5 percent). A symmetric control of 1,260 captains from non-China voyages on the same pages yields the same phenomenon in other trades. The documented overlap is therefore a verified minimum, not evidence that the China trade absorbed wartime personnel preferentially. Preprint; submitted to the Journal of the Early Republic, October 2026.

detail.abstract: "This paper studies how elections shape political communication. We formulate a theory of electoral competition with costly communication. If opposite candidates reach different audiences with their messages, they diverge and seek to polarize the electorate. We then analyze Twitter/X communication by 367 political leaders in 21 countries during 2013-2022, focusing on competition between populists and non-populists. Following Gentzkow, Shapiro and Taddy (2019), we estimate a structural model of speech and show that political rhetoric becomes more polarized before the election. This reflects two main theoretical mechanisms: politicians increasingly emphasize issues distinctive of their type, and within each issue, they use more extreme language."

detail.abstract: Perceived transit affordability is often assessed through fare levels, expenditure-to-income ratios, or broad satisfaction measures. These approaches are informative but do not fully explain why travelers facing similar fares and financial circumstances may evaluate affordability differently in practice. This study examines perceived transit affordability as a distinct evaluative outcome shaped by individual resources, fare assistance, transit-use exposure, perceived non-price service quality, household vehicle availability, and objective neighborhood transit supply. Weighted ordered-logit models were estimated using regional transportation survey data from northeastern Illinois, with sequential specifications used to assess the contribution of financial, behavioral, service-related, and contextual factors. Interaction models were then used to evaluate whether affordability relationships varied across age, transit-use frequency, and household vehicle availability. The results show that financial resources and participation in fare-assistance programs are relevant, but they provide only a partial explanation of perceived affordability. The largest improvement in model performance occurred after perceived non-price transit-service quality was introduced. More favorable evaluations of reliability, punctuality, accessibility, transfers, cleanliness, seating, passenger information, and the ability of transit to meet travel needs were strongly associated with higher perceived affordability. Objective neighborhood transit-service intensity also had an independent positive association, indicating that both experienced service quality and the amount of transit service available near home contribute to affordability evaluations. The interaction results reveal important heterogeneity. Affordability declined with age among respondents who used transit rarely or occasionally, but increased with age among regular users. The positive association between service quality and affordability was also stronger among zero-vehicle households, suggesting that service performance matters most when private transportation alternatives are limited. These findings show that transit affordability depends not only on the price paid, but also on the practical mobility value obtained. Effective affordability policy should therefore combine fare assistance with improvements in service quality, reliability, and neighborhood service availability.

detail.abstract: This study examines the extent to which small states exercise meaningful influence in the international world order despite their limited population and territorial size. Traditional theories of international relations associate influence with military and economic capabilities. Consequently, this results in the assumption of a limited capacity to shape pivotal international outcomes by smaller states. Through a comparative analysis of Singapore and Qatar, this paper investigates how small states overcame their population and territorial size to be important states in the world, applying realism, liberalism, and constructivism, emphasizing strategic economic actions and diplomacy and drawing upon realist and liberal perspectives. This paper argues that while population and territorial size can create significant limitations, they do not solely determine international influence. Findings indicate that smaller states can project significant functional power when they occupy critical roles in international networks. However, this influence remains conditional, as during military operations and other conflicts that arise in the world, the interests of major economic and military powers are prioritised. This contributes to the broader debate concerning the nature of power and influence within the current international system. States with smaller populations and territorial sizes may successfully influence international politics through diplomacy and economic specialisation, appealing to international organisations and markets. However, this influence declines during armed conflicts, as military power provides structural and geopolitical power in today's world.
